title: Operations
intro.1: Updating, removing, reaching the admin from elsewhere, and what restarts do.
update.title: Update
update.1: With the installer: the latest one moves your installation to the release it names, pulling that release’s images, and removes the images of the release before once the new one runs.
update.2: Every run of the installer, with --update or without, also adds Google’s newest Chrome stable from Google’s signed repository to the browser image when there is one. When that changes a session image, or the controller has to start again, it starts the controller and the admin afresh, which ends the sessions running at the time; otherwise they keep running. When Google’s newest Chrome declares other dependencies than the release’s browser image was built for, the installer stops and says so, leaving easi.run running as it was: the next release’s image follows them.
update.3: Installed by hand: in the checkout, pull, rebuild, then start the controller and the admin afresh, so new sessions use the new images. Compose reads compose.override.yaml on its own.
update.4: Restarting the admin stops every running session and ends every login: it removes whatever an earlier run left behind before it accepts new sessions.
remove.title: Remove
remove.1: After you confirm (--yes confirms ahead, for an agent), the installer removes what it put on the server: easi.run’s containers, with every session, its volumes, networks and images, the docker.service drop-in and the firewall rule, and the TCP settings it made, putting back the values they replaced (unless another easi.run installation on the server still needs them), its files in ~/.config/easi-run (the directory too, when nothing else is left in it), and Claude Code’s easi server when it is this installation’s. It keeps the checkout, ~/easi.run, with any .env or override file in it, Docker’s build cache, which docker builder prune removes for every project on the server, and the Debian image its root steps ran in, which it names.
reaching-the-admin.title: Reaching the admin
reaching-the-admin.1: By default the Compose file publishes it on the host’s 127.0.0.1:9443 only. From another machine, use the command you already use to log in to the server, adding -N -L 9443:127.0.0.1:9443 (for example ssh -N -L 9443:127.0.0.1:9443 you@your-server), then open https://localhost:9443.
reaching-the-admin.2: Behind your own domain or reverse proxy, set ADMIN_ORIGIN to the exact address people open and add the name to ADMIN_HOSTNAMES, in an override file: compose.yaml sets both itself. A change, a login or a viewer from any other origin is refused.
reaching-the-admin.3: To use your own certificate, put tls-cert.pem and tls-key.pem in the admin’s state volume.
reaching-the-admin.4: After you change ADMIN_HOSTNAMES, the next start makes the admin's own certificate again for the new names. A certificate you put in the state volume yourself is never replaced; without its key, the admin stops and says so.
reach-the-admin-from.title: Reach the admin from anywhere
reach-the-admin-from.1: Without an SSH tunnel, you can put one of these in front of the admin, each with your own account. Exposing the admin beyond the server is your choice. Either way, set ADMIN_ORIGIN to the address you will open, then run bash ~/easi.run/install.sh again. Logins then work at that address only, and a passkey made at another hostname does not sign in there.
tailscale.title: Tailscale
tailscale.1: On the server, in your tailnet, with HTTPS certificates turned on for it, this serves the admin at https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net (that address is your ADMIN_ORIGIN), to your tailnet only: serve shares within the tailnet, and Funnel, which publishes to the internet, is not used. The admin stays on the server’s 127.0.0.1; https+insecure means Tailscale does not check the admin’s own certificate on that loopback hop.
cloudflare-tunnel-with-cloudflare.title: Cloudflare Tunnel with Cloudflare Access
cloudflare-tunnel-with-cloudflare.1: On a domain in your Cloudflare account, first add a Cloudflare Access application for the name (in Cloudflare One: Access controls, Applications, Create new application, Self-hosted and private, with the name as its public hostname), with an Allow policy for your own email: Access checks who you are before any request reaches the admin’s login page. Then, on the server, create the tunnel and give it the name:
cloudflare-tunnel-with-cloudflare.2: Save its configuration, with the tunnel’s id that create printed: cloudflared reaches the admin on the server’s loopback and checks its certificate against the copy the installer keeps.
cloudflare-tunnel-with-cloudflare.4: What protects the admin then: who may reach the address at all (your tailnet’s devices, or your Access policy), then the admin’s sign-in: your password and, when you turned it on, the second step, or a passkey.
viewers-far-from-the.title: Viewers far from the server
viewers-far-from-the.1: easi.run sends a viewer only as much of the screen as its connection delivers within its round trip and a little more, so a slow or distant connection gets fewer frames rather than late ones. Two things then keep the stream smooth on a long or lossy path, and both are automatic.
the-media-over-udp.title: The media over UDP
the-media-over-udp.1: Where UDP gets through, the viewer’s media (the picture, the pointer and the sound) take a WebTransport session on the admin’s UDP port, 9443/udp, beside the HTTPS connection, which keeps everything else. Its congestion control is BBR, which keeps the rate a lossy path can carry. The viewer tries it as it connects and again every 30 seconds while it has none; where UDP does not get through (a firewall, a network that blocks it), everything stays on HTTPS, as before. The installer tells the admin the IPv4 address you reached the server at over SSH, and Docker publishes the port, past host firewalls such as ufw. If your provider has a firewall for the server (a Hetzner Cloud Firewall, an AWS security group, a Google Cloud VPC rule, an Oracle security list), let 9443/udp through it. To give another address (your server’s Tailscale address, say), set it in .env and run bash ~/easi.run/install.sh again; installed by hand, without the installer, the media stay on HTTPS until .env sets one, and ADMIN_UDP_BIND=0.0.0.0 to publish the port beyond the server’s loopback:
the-server-s-tcp.title: The server’s TCP
the-server-s-tcp.1: How the server’s TCP carries the HTTPS connection is up to its kernel, and Linux’s defaults suit nearby clients. CUBIC, the default, does not pace what it sends unless the fq queue does, so what its window allows leaves at the server’s line rate, and a shallow queue on a long path drops much of a large burst, after which CUBIC sends far less for a while; and a connection idle for a moment starts again from a small window, so an update after a pause takes several round trips. BBR paces what it sends at about the rate the path delivers (with the fq queue, which BBR’s authors recommend, or by itself on recent kernels), and keeping the window across pauses lets an update after a pause go at once. When the kernel has BBR, the installer sets these, now and at every boot, in this file (and loads tcp_bbr at boot, from /etc/modules-load.d/easi-run.conf); without BBR it leaves TCP as it is:
the-server-s-tcp.2: The file also keeps the values it replaced, which bash install.sh --uninstall puts back. These settings are the whole host’s, for every TCP connection it makes. The congestion control applies to connections opened afterwards (reconnect the tunnel and reload the viewer), and default_qdisc to interfaces set up afterwards: until the next reboot, an existing interface keeps its queue unless you replace it (sudo tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq, with your interface’s name). logs.title: Logs
logs.1: docker compose finds the installation from its checkout, ~/easi.run; from anywhere else, docker logs easi-run-admin-1 and docker logs easi-run-controller-1 show the same.
logs.2: The admin logs its certificate’s fingerprint on every start.
